headline: Testosterone’s label
just changed.
dek: FDA dropped the heart-risk boxed warning in 2025 and added a blood pressure warning.
photoAlt: A night-shift plant operator in a reflective work shirt sits at a table with his hard hat and paperwork.
byline: Adonis Men’s Health · Checked Oct 31, 2026 · Clinical review pending

pull.quote: is approved solely for use in men who lack or have low testosterone levels in conjunction with an associated medical condition.

body: On February 28, 2025, FDA told the makers of every [[/testosterone|testosterone]] product in the United States to rewrite their labels.[^fda25] The agency had finished reviewing a large heart-safety trial called TRAVERSE, along with blood pressure studies it had required years earlier. It asked companies to add the trial’s results to every label and to begin “removing language from the Boxed Warning related to an increased risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes for all testosterone products.”[^fda25] In the same notice, FDA required new or updated blood pressure warnings, because the completed studies “confirmed an increase in blood pressure with use of all testosterone products, class-wide.”[^fda25]

The label change did not turn testosterone into a general wellness drug. FDA’s notice says testosterone “is approved solely for use in men who lack or have low testosterone levels in conjunction with an associated medical condition.”[^fda25] The approved forms now include gels, a skin patch, a system that sticks to the gum, injections and capsules taken by mouth.[^fda25] Testosterone undecanoate, one of those forms, was approved as the Aveed injection in 2014 and as the Jatenzo capsule in 2019.[^aveed][^jatenzo]

TRAVERSE was the evidence behind the change. It enrolled 5,246 men aged 45 to 80 who had heart disease or a high risk of it, symptoms of low testosterone and two low blood tests, and gave them a daily testosterone gel or a placebo gel.[^traverse] Heart attack, stroke or death from heart causes occurred in 7.0% of the men on testosterone and 7.3% on placebo.[^traverse] The authors concluded that testosterone “was noninferior to placebo with respect to the incidence of major adverse cardiac events.”[^traverse] Noninferior means it was not worse by a set margin; the trial was built to test heart safety, not whether testosterone helps symptoms.

Other problems did show up. The AndroGel 1.62% label now reports that in TRAVERSE, atrial fibrillation occurred in 3.5% of men on testosterone and 2.4% on placebo, and acute kidney injury in 2.3% and 1.5%.[^androgel] A separate analysis of 5,204 of the same men looked at broken bones. Fractures occurred in 3.50% of the testosterone group and 2.46% of the placebo group, and the researchers wrote that testosterone “did not result in a lower incidence of clinical fracture than placebo.”[^fracture]

Some parts of the label did not change at all. FDA kept its “Limitation of Use”[^fda25] language on aging. The AndroGel label says that safety and efficacy in men whose testosterone is low only because of age “have not been established,”[^androgel] so that use is off-label. Testosterone remains a Schedule III controlled substance under federal law.[^dea] Compounded creams and sprays are not FDA approved; FDA does not review compounded drugs for safety, effectiveness or quality before they are sold.[^compq]

Fertility is where many men first run into trouble. The label warns that with large doses, “spermatogenesis may be suppressed through feedback inhibition of pituitary FSH,”[^androgel] which can lower sperm count. The clearest measure of that effect comes from a 1990 World Health Organization study that tested weekly testosterone injections as a male contraceptive. Of 271 healthy, fertile men in ten centres across seven countries, 157 stopped producing sperm in three semen samples in a row.[^who]

That is why three other drugs come up so often around testosterone. The first, [[/enclomiphene|enclomiphene]], is not approved by any regulator we checked. The European Medicines Agency refused it in 2018. Its committee noted that the studies “did not look at whether EnCyzix would improve symptoms such as bone strength, weight gain, impotence and libido.”[^emaqa] The agency’s assessment counted four blood-clot events in men taking it, one of them a fatal ischaemic stroke.[^emaar] In June 2022, FDA’s compounding advisory committee voted 8 to 4 against putting enclomiphene on the list of substances pharmacies may compound from.[^pcac22] It remains in FDA’s category of nominated substances still under evaluation.[^cat1]

The second, [[/anastrozole|anastrozole]], lowers estrogen. Its label is narrow: “ARIMIDEX is indicated for adjuvant treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer.”[^arimidex] Every approved use is in women, so use in men is off-label. In a one-year randomized trial in older men with low or borderline testosterone, spine bone density fell on anastrozole compared with placebo.[^burnett]

The third is [[/hcg|hCG]], a hormone that acts much like the pituitary signal to the testes. Its label lists undescended testes in boys, some cases of low testosterone from a pituitary problem, and ovulation in women.[^novarel] Taking it alongside testosterone is off-label, and the studies of that use are small: a three-week trial in healthy men that measured testosterone inside the testis,[^coviello] and a review of the records of 26 men.[^hsieh] Since March 23, 2020, hCG has been regulated as a biologic, and FDA says such products “are not eligible for the exemptions for compounded drugs under sections 503A and 503B of the FD&C Act.”[^notice]

Two more groups of products sit near this lane. [[/clomiphene|Clomiphene]], the older fertility drug that contains enclomiphene, is indicated “for the treatment of ovulatory dysfunction in women desiring pregnancy,”[^clomid] and its use in men is off-label. Then there are the SARMs, such as [[/enobosarm|enobosarm]], [[/rad-140|RAD-140]] and [[/lgd-4033|LGD-4033]], which are often sold online. FDA says SARMs “are considered unapproved drugs,”[^sarms] and that they “cannot be legally marketed in the U.S. as a dietary supplement or drug at this time.”[^sarms]

Much is still unknown. TRAVERSE did not test whether testosterone improves energy, mood or sex drive, and no large trial has tested hCG given with testosterone. The enclomiphene trials measured hormones and sperm, not symptoms. For athletes the answer is simpler: testosterone is on the World Anti-Doping Agency’s list, banned at all times.[^wada]
